profile.reading: Apple Inc. operates a data center campus in Prineville, Crook County, Oregon, first announced by the company on February 21, 2012, when Apple said it would build a "Green Data Center" on a roughly 160-acre tract of land it owns in the city, per Wikipedia's article on Prineville. Since the late 2000s, Apple has invested more than $1 billion across multiple data center buildings within Prineville city limits, per the same source; the campus has grown from its original building into a multi-building complex over the following decade, of which this registry maps four separate structures, numbered here only by their position west to east across the site since no individually confirmed building names or codes have been located this session. This building sits at Southwest Baldwin Road, Prineville, Crook County, Oregon, 97554, an address derived from reverse-geocoding this record's own OpenStreetMap coordinates rather than confirmed directly by Apple; Apple's own site and newsroom archive do not publish individual street addresses, square footage, IT capacity, or opening-year figures broken out by building for the Prineville campus, and a Baxtel directory listing for the facility, found in an earlier research pass, confirms only the 97754 ZIP code while keeping its own address behind a contact-request form rather than publishing it. Multiple additional research attempts this session to reach data center trade-press and directory sites for building-specific figures (DatacenterDynamics, Data Center Knowledge, DataCenterHawk) returned either 404 errors on guessed URLs or were blocked by the sites' own access rules, so no further building-level detail could be added beyond what is stated here. Crook County has drawn several data center developments in the years since Apple's original announcement, owing in part to the region's cool climate, available land, and renewable power access from the Pacific Northwest grid, though this registry does not attribute that broader trend to any single building on this specific campus. Data Center Dynamics reported in 2016 that Apple planned a third Prineville building of about 330,000 square feet, matching the size of the two buildings already standing or under construction on the 154 acre campus at that time, and noted the addition would bring the total number of data centers in the surrounding Prineville corridor, including two operated separately by Facebook, to six. Apples plans for the campus also included a dedicated logistics and distribution building, an on-site power substation, and a wastewater treatment plant that Apple said it would make available to other users on reasonable terms, expected to save about five million gallons of water annually once operational in spring 2018.

reading.body:
Apple operates a large data center campus in Prineville, Crook County, Oregon that the company announced in 2012 on roughly 160 acres it owns. The campus appears on this registry as four separate rows with generic names and no distinguishing building labels, but no specific street address or individual building capacity figures are published by Apple. The research note indicates the campus location is confirmed but its internal structure and power allocation across buildings remain opaque to external view.

Oregon has 133 mapped data center facilities, of which only 8 publish power capacity figures totaling 156.6 MW. This Apple campus ranks ninth among all Oregon facilities by published megawatts, but that ranking reflects only the eight facilities with disclosed capacity. The true position of Apple's Prineville campus in the state's infrastructure hierarchy cannot be determined from published data.

The absence of published capacity means this site cannot translate Apple's Prineville footprint into racks or accelerator equivalents, assess its role in state-level AI infrastructure, or compare it to other campuses. For a reader evaluating whether this campus matters to AI scaling, the only usable fact is that Apple owns a substantial 160-acre campus in Oregon that has existed for over a decade. Whether it serves AI workloads, what power it draws, or how much of the state's compute infrastructure it represents remains unknown.
